#6664. Testing, Testing! The Vogue Beauty Board Puts Fall’s Buzziest Beauty Products to the Test

Testing, testing—beauty product testing, that is! A quick trip to the beauty closet would reveal that deliveries are never scarce—with our mail room frequently depositing everything from forthcoming launches to restocks of longstanding favorites to the shelves of Vogue’s beauty team. Dare go on a holiday, and editors will find a mountain of deliveries waiting to be unboxed when they return (enough to earn a spot on the reality TV show Hoarders, or, if you’re like me, trigger your eco-anxiety). Yes, it’s a champagne problem to have, which is why we are sharing the wealth with our fellow Vogue Beauty Board members to broaden the scope of perspective.

So, what to test, and where to even begin? There’s skincare, makeup, haircare (and more)—oh my! Everyone’s got favorite categories—sometimes our product picks are driven by preference. Take Vogue’s beauty shopping editor, Kiana Murden who will never say no to a lip balm; or perhaps necessity sparks the insatiable urge to discover—I have found a new favorite finishing oil to add shine to my just-blown out hair.

As for our newly-established Beauty Board—our community of experts, founders, and board-certified practitioners—they will test a carefully curated batch of products and share their candid take. Below a look at what we tested. Check back each month to see what we’ve been trying.

About the Product: Dior’s skin tint is a triple-threat—complexion coverage, SPF protection, and a skincare-infused formula. To start, it comes in 24 shades, all offering light to medium coverage. Ingredients like fermented collagen, glycerin, and vitamin E hydrate skin for seamless application, while hybrid sunscreen ingredients offer protection up to SPF 20.

About the Product: Yep, Hermès does beauty too—and their lip mask leaves your pout soft and supple. Made in Italy with 97% naturally-derived ingredients, Hermes’s lip mask repairs chapped lips with hyaluronic acid, sesame seed extract, ceramides, and astaxanthin (that’s where that orange hue comes from).

About the Product: CurrentBody’s latest LED mask innovation elevates the brand’s existing library of tech. Series 3 has had a major boost in bulbs from 236 to 750, designed to treat everything from hyperpigmentation to fine lines. Board-certified nurse practitioner Natia Rufolo particularly likes its customization features: “It incorporates six wavelengths, including 633-nanometer red, 830-nanometer near-infrared, and 1072-nanometer deep near-infrared, alongside blue, green, and yellow light, so it goes beyond a traditional red-and-near-infrared mask,” she said in our best red light therapy guide.

About the Product: Jones Road’s brightening concealer uses a trio of botanical extracts (marshmallow root, rice bran, and licorice root) to help brighten discoloration while offering buildable medium coverage. Meanwhile, shea butter allows the dense, creamy formula to sink into the skin for an entirely natural, non-cakey finish—and for even more coverage, this pick pairs well with the brand’s neutralizer.

About the Product: A follow up to TIRTIR’s viral semi-matte cushion foundation, its Tinted Skin Glow Cushion offers a luminous alternative. Here, the formula features 73% skin-care ingredients and a serum-like texture that just bounces into the complexion. A blend of niacinamide, peptides, hyaluronic acid, and botanical oils deliver hydrating, plumping benefits while offering medium, buildable coverage.

About the Product: La Mer offers some of the most prestigious skincare on the market—in both price and formulation. Aside from the brand’s signature concentrated Miracle Broth (a blend of fermented kelp extract, vitamins, and nutrients), The Concentrate brings together lime tea concentrate and botanic oils to soothe irritated skin—whether you’re combating general redness or post-procedural skin.

About the Product: Christophe Robin’s lightweight dry oil does a bit of everything—hydrates, adds shine, and keeps frizz in check. Use it before styling for heat protection, or after to boost shine and smooth flyaways. The formula combines amla, coconut, tung wood, and oat oils, plus skincare-quality ingredients like squalane and ceramides, to leave your hair feeling soft and healthy.

About the Product: Part skin tint, part mineral sunscreen, Carte Blanche’s Multi-Hyphenate offers sheer complexion coverage with a barely-there feel. The star ingredient, exosomes derived from licorice and flax plant, helps brighten hyperpigmentation, while vitamin C and bakuchiol offer added antioxidant support. Plus, squalane and panthenol soothe and smooth dehydrated skin.

About the Product: Stubborn breakouts and irritated complexions are no match for Serum Vivant. Inspired by Biologique Recherche’s best-selling Masque Vivant, this formula treats adult blemishes through a mix of prebiotics, postbiotics, and fermented extracts to support the skin’s microbiome, sans dryness or discomfort.

About the Product: SK-II lovers to the front! There’s a new serum to know. Introducing its Facial Treatment Serum—infused with “boosting oil pearls” rich with vitamin E and castor oil, bursting upon application to dispense the perfect amount of product without loosing a lightweight feel. Then, niacinamide and galactomyces ferment filtrate (GFF) are in the mix too for added brightening.

About the Product: 111Skin’s rinse-off peel exfoliates with a blend of AHAs, BHAs, PHAs, and botanical extracts. Papain (AKA papaya enzymes) and milk thistle extract help to slough off dead skin and brighten hyperpigmentation. Meanwhile, glutathione helps fight against oxidative stress.

About the Product: L’Oréal Paris offers an affordable moisturizer that balances active ingredients alongside hydrating humectants. The super-rich texture applies like butter, combining hyaluronic acid to boost water retention, retinol to smooth skin and target signs of aging, and vitamin C to brighten your complexion. The good news, though, is that it’s safe for sensitive skin, given retinol and vitamin C’s relatively low concentration.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

We selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, type, texture, packaging, finish, and the concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6663. Fear of God Fall 2027 Ready-to-Wear

After spending almost a year with his design team in Paris, Jerry Lorenzo moved it back to Los Angeles, while continuing to develop Fear of God’s collections in Milan: “I just felt like—creatively, emotionally—I needed to be rooted in my city,” he said. The decision influenced TEN, his latest collection and the tenth numbered offering in thirteen years. “It doesn't have the cleanliness of Paris,” he acknowledged. The designer hadn't planned for the tenth collection to mark any particular milestone, but described its timing as “providential,” considering the spiritual significance of the number. Bringing together everything from tailoring to vintage-inspired sportswear, he left nothing out: Or, as he put it: “To say something that's unequivocally yours, you have to put all of you into it.”

There was no particular theme this season. Lorenzo cited everything from Keanu Reeves in flannel to Michael Jordan in a suit to Allen Iverson walking into a basketball game among the references that have long informed his work. Instead, the inspiration came from “knowing who we are,” he said. Having navigated what he described as a difficult year, he considers TEN one of his most emotional collections, shaped as much by setbacks as by successes. As a young brand, Fear of God had sometimes tried to “serve an industry,” rather than its own audience: “It's easy to get lost there,” Lorenzo said.

The tailoring was generous yet controlled: long black overcoats layered over grey waistcoats and wide trousers, cropped leather jackets paired with fluid suiting, and softly structured blazers with exaggerated shoulders. A belted black leather coat came with bright red gloves, while quilted leather jackets, faded denim, and washed workwear introduced more rugged textures. The palette moved between black, charcoal, olive, earthy browns and washed-out blue, punctuated by flashes of red. Alongside familiar wool-cashmere fabrics and American jersey, Lorenzo introduced velour, new leathers and “a lot of Japanese fabrics,” including denim and canvas. Bonded details and articulated sleeves added structure to the oversized silhouettes.

The American influence was particularly evident in Athletics, the category rooted in Lorenzo's personal approach to sportswear: “I don't ever put anything technical on,” he said of his gym wardrobe. The collection also introduces the Fear of God Trainer, the brand's first athletic shoe developed entirely in-house, with supercritical foam cushioning. Rather than relying on conspicuous branding, Lorenzo believes its identity is immediately recognizable through its design: “Shape and materials are undeniably ours.” After years of collaborations with sportswear partners, the experience brought less a lesson than a realization: “You kind of realize you could have done it on your own the whole time.”

#6662. Gordon Ramsay’s Routine for a Six-Pack at 60 Includes Daily Crunches and Red-Light Therapy

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

At home in London, he shows me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he says. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”

Ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he says.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”

“It’s not physically hard with big weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”

“What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, currently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”

“I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”

“10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”

“From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”

“I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”

“I’m big on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”

“I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”

“I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”

“Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone said the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”

“Sign up for something. Have a target because that gets you out of bed, with a bigger, incentivized plan. I need that target twice a year, every six months. And I’ve done that since my 40th birthday. Whether it’s half an Ironman, whether it’s a marathon, half a marathon, I’ve always got something to focus on.”

“No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”

#6660. A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

Arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

The Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

We’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

On a crisp mid-November morning, Anthony Boyle arrived to the podcast studio wearing a leather jacket, or as our Head of Editorial Content, Chloe Malle, called it “Jensen’s jacket”—a reference to the signature leather jacket donned by disgraced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. The two of them portray the nerdy genius couple that made it big during the cryptocurrency boom and then met their spectacular undoing after being caught stealing billions from customers.

Unlike many of his previous roles—which had him portraying mustachioed Irishmen in period garb—Boyle spoke about the source material he mined in service of his transformation into this awkward American mastermind. “There was a lot of footage of him. The lad loved giving interviews,” Boyle explained, “Even at the collapse [of the company], when all the lawyers were like, ‘Stop giving interviews,’ he was like, ‘Just one more…’”

Boyle once attended a Los Angeles warehouse party with some “crypto lads” as a form of character study. “I thought there was something really interesting in that no one had ever looked at these guys. These were guys who were in their mothers’ basement, and they suddenly became billionaires. Suddenly they had power, and they had money, which in America makes you a god. If you have money in Ireland, it makes you a wanker,” he laughed, “I do think he truly believed in effective altruism, but, you know, the best laid plans of mice and men gang aft agley.”

They also discussed several of his other roles from his Broadway debut in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child to his beloved performance in Say Nothing. He reminisced about his years living in midtown Manhattan, including a “great little Irish bar in Port Authority.” During his rare moments of downtime, he’s been known to watch reality television. “Anything with ‘love’ in the title, I’ll watch.”

#6656. Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

Turns out, set-it-and-forget-it has its limits.

With busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.

But think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you plan a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.

Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” says Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.

Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”

“The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.

“The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”

What happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.

“Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch says. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”

Cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” says White.

The ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.

Smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.

“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch says.

The answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.

The safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.

Our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch says.

No time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.

It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

#6655. On the Front Lines of the Advent Calendar Wars

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the mysterious hackers hitting refrigeration systems.

I’m starting today’s Open Tab with my favorite thing in the world: a morsel of exclusive news. In chatting with BA alum Alison Roman about First Bloom, her soon-to-open NYC storefront (more on that from me very soon), she told me she’s releasing a new podcast that will be officially announced early next week.

I’m mostly sworn to secrecy until Roman drops the trailer, but I can tell you there will be cooking, there will be guests, and there will be banter. But, she said, this project will be distinctly different from her earlier work. “I’m not going back to Home Movies. I’m just not,” she told me over the phone earlier this week.

Also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

Gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data shows search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

Part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

But drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

If you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a new gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

In a report from The New York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

The saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you plan a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

Former Bon Appétit food editor Andy Baraghani is likely familiar to readers of this publication. But now, after years of cooking for others—on the line at Chez Panisse, here in the Test Kitchen—he’s opening his own restaurant, Ditto, in Union Square. “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see,” he told Ella Quittner, who profiled him for BA. Read on to see how Baraghani’s vision comes to life at his first ever restaurant.

Jeans, a tee, a great sweater, and good boots. Simple and comfortable, but still put together. For this trip, I brought my Blundstones—perfect with denim, corduroy, and all the cozy layers.

My Louis Vuitton makeup bag always comes with me, whether I’m flying or driving. It keeps my beauty essentials together and brings a little of my home routine with me wherever I’m staying.

Both, actually. I love a good sweater and a scarf—I’m always happy to have an extra layer. For this trip, I packed my Toteme scarf along with plenty of knitwear.

Lesse face spray—it’s a staple in my travel beauty bag.

I keep accessories pretty minimal. My Tiffany & Co. watch is my go-to for every day, so it comes with me everywhere. I also brought a black leather belt with silver hardware that I know works well with both jeans and corduroy pants.

No—I gravitate toward fabrics that need very little maintenance. I like being able to unpack, get dressed, and enjoy wherever I am without too much fuss.

My Blundstone boots! They’re the pair I reach for for a few days in the countryside. I love them with corduroy, a plaid shirt, and an oversized sweater.

My Toteme scarf. I wear it around my head or neck, either draped open or tied in a knot. It’s really beautiful, and changing how I wear it gives the same outfit a different feeling. I love it with a simple tee and sweater or tucked into a jacket when it’s particularly cold.

#6652. The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting new pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

When companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical company DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that says “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s important to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

Ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year

About ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That said, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

Our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 1,100ºFWarranty: Lifetime

About carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

Our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats quickly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

About stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat quickly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

Read more about our favorite cast-iron pans.

Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt.Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: NoOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

Our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

Read more about our favorite Dutch ovens.

Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

The bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That said, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

#6651. A New Book Explores the Lessons We Can All Learn From Indigenous Wellness Traditions

The global wellness industry has reached a fever pitch—and shows no signs of slowing down. Overstimulated, under-rested, and on the brink of burnout, we’re desperately seeking antidotes to the ills of the digital era. But what if the answers to our modern-day woes lie in ancient Native American wisdom, not in a supposed cure-all gadget, supplement, or fitness routine?

For millennia, Indigenous communities have prioritized connection to nature, practiced reciprocity with community, and upheld sacred cultural traditions. We can all embrace these holistic principles in our daily lives, says Lakota/Anishinaabe wellness advocate Chelsey Luger. That’s the premise behind her new book, Native Home: The Ancestral Art of Creating Healing Spaces. In it, she offers tangible ways to incorporate these concepts into our living spaces to promote mental, physical, spiritual, and emotional balance.

“Everybody in North America should understand Native American home teachings because we’re all living on this land,” says Luger, who is an enrolled member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa and a descendant of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. “There’s a movement in the home industry right now centered around ensuring our surroundings support our well-being. This might be an emerging conversation in the wellness space, but Indigenous communities have been living this way for centuries.”

Luger and her husband, Onk Akimel O’odham fitness educator Thosh Collins, co-founded the grassroots initiative Well For Culture back in 2013, with the aim of revitalizing Indigenous wellness practices. Since then, they’ve been traveling to tribal nations across the country to both teach and learn from these communities. Native Home is the culmination of those lessons.

She underscores that these principles are applicable to everyone, no matter their heritage, with this caveat: The difference between appreciation and appropriation is all in the approach. “I’m not encouraging you to do exactly what Indigenous communities do,” she says. “I’m encouraging you to apply these teachings to your own home in a way that reflects your own culture.”

For example, in a Native worldview, every home should tell a story through its design and decor, Luger explains. Her ancestors painted their tepees with images representing their familial experiences. Similarly, the artwork adorning our walls should feel curated and specific to our identity.

With this in mind, Luger encourages people to stay intimately involved in their home’s design and decorating process, as she’s doing with her family’s in-the-works house on Arizona’s Salt River Reservation (where Collins is from). But you needn’t be building a new abode to reap the benefits of Indigenous wellness. There are easy, everyday ways to embrace these principles—and they don’t cost a thing.

Starting small is as simple as decluttering one room to reduce sensory overload, letting in more natural sunlight to balance circadian rhythms, opening up your windows for cross-drafting airflow, or carving out an area for movement—even if it’s only a designated stretching space. Next-level applications encompass philosophies like Indigenous minimalism and Native geomancy (auspicious arrangement, akin to feng shui), which are all explained in the book.

Like most Indigenous wisdom, Luger’s advice is pretty intuitive—and yet, it isn’t how we lead our lives today. “We might say that we don’t want to overconsume, but Americans tend to think the bigger the house, the better,” she says. “Our generation is facing a housing crisis, and we should all embrace smaller living. Not only is it easier to maintain, but it keeps us better connected. That’s what this is ultimately about: interconnection.”

Here, Luger offers five tips for incorporating Indigenous wellness in your home.

“We’ve always had a respect for the elements—air, fire, water, and earth. Air in particular is considered sacred by most Indigenous communities. Here in the United States, we use air conditioning more than most other countries in the world. It’s a wonderful luxury, but our indoor environments should better reflect the outdoors. Try keeping your windows open for part of the day, no matter the season.”

“Doorways are considered portals, which are places of high energy. Growing up, my dad would hang a hand drum or a medicine wheel above our door. It’s a way to bring good energy both for those arriving and for those leaving. Honor the doorway by hanging something that represents the presence of your ancestors and offers both protection and peace.”

“It’s a very European idea to have a separate room for everything. In contrast, Indigenous homes historically tended to be more fluid, with communal rooms that foster togetherness. That interconnection is part of our values as Indigenous people. Let at least one space in your home feel more multi-use, where family members can share space.”

“Many traditional Native structures are round, which represents women, Mother Earth, and our egalitarian values. Indigenous architect Douglas Cardinal (Métis/Blackfoot), who designed the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., often expresses this with curvilinear forms. But you don’t have to build a round house or room. Choose a circular dining table, rugs, and pillows rather than square or rectangular ones.”

“As Native people, we’ve never lost that closeness to our ancestors, even through colonization and the boarding school era. That spiritual and practical connection to who we are as people is just part of our culture. Whoever you are, wherever you come from—everybody has ancestors they can and should feel connected to. Take time to learn about your culture, and then make your home a reflection of that.”

#6650. The 10 Best Lessons I Learned From My First Year Living Alone

The other night, while I was two glasses deep into a bottle of natural wine, sitting on my couch in my Hollywood studio in front of The Simpsons, when I wondered: had either of my grandmothers ever had the opportunity to live like this? Alone but (mostly) not lonely, in a space completely their own, with nobody vying for their labor or attention or filling the silence? I moved into my own place just over a year ago after a breakup with a live-in partner, and while I hesitate to go full loneliness influencer, I’m grateful for the series of privileges and twists of fate that have brought me to the highs, lows and everyday mediums of solo living.

It turns out Virginia Woolf wasn’t lying when she wrote about the importance of a woman having a room of her own, or, as Destiny’s Child so memorably put it: “The watch I'm wearing (I bought it), the house I live in (I bought it), the car I'm driving (I bought it), I depend on me (I depend on me).” To be fair, I rent my studio, I don’t wear a watch, and my 2013 Hyundai Sonata is covered in dents, but the motto still applies. Below are ten lessons I learned from my first year living alone in Los Angeles.

I’ve garnered a not-unearned reputation among my friends for bailing a little more frequently than I should, and while that’s a bad habit no matter who you cohabitate with, living alone has taught me that I need to treat my social engagements—whether they’re set-in-stone events or casual movie dates—with the same commitment I bring to work obligations. My friends deserve it, and just as importantly, I deserve to see and enjoy myself amongst actual human beings every day, especially now that I can’t count on automatic social interaction at home.

Do you own a drill? Me neither. When I moved into my studio last fall, I told myself I would become the kind of person who initiated her own D.I.Y. projects and fixed things when they broke without a) crying or b) live-documenting it on Instagram—but as it turns out, I’m still me, and even the newfound independence of solo living hasn’t made me handier. I’d like to build my skills in this arena, but until I do, I've realized that it’s a lot easier and more joy-inducing to pay a helpful friend I refer to as my “handybutch” to hang my art, install my Tulip shades and turn on my pilot light than it is to farm out the jobs to a random TaskRabbit…or sit around waiting for myself to suddenly become amazing at using a level. Sure, money’s tighter now that I don’t split bills with a roommate, but investing in own comfort in my living space feels worth it.

I’ve always known this to be true when it comes to fashion (don’t talk to me unless I’ve got a proper ‘fit on…literally, please do not), but when I lived with roommates or my ex, it was easier for me to surrender control of my living environment—a.k.a. be a slob—and only complete the amount of chores that resulted in nobody passive-aggressively texting me to please clean the bathroom. Now that I live alone, I’m the only one affected by my messiness, and as it turns out, I value myself enough to try to combat it where possible, whether that means making my bed every day for the first time in my life or doing my dishes immediately so that I don’t attract bugs.

On that bug note…yes, I’m more of a proponent of the ‘pay someone to do the hard things’ theory of solo living, but there are some hard things you can’t and arguably shouldn’t outsource, and for me, Hard Thing #1 is definitely dealing with insects. I’ve been lucky enough to only ever spot two water bugs in my apartment over the last year (which a very patient exterminator told me did not “constitute an infestation”), but both times, I wept and dry-heaved and instinctually went through my mental Rolodex of who I could call to kill them before…growing the hell up and killing them myself. Do I particularly want to put this new life skill into play a third time? No, but at least I know I can if I have to.

Okay, I stole this quote from Joan Didion, but when you live alone, the days and nights can collapse into themselves without a real sense of occasion…unless you proactively create said occasion, something I try to do every time I light an expensive candle or stick of incense instead of “saving it for later” or start chopping onions for that complex Bolognese recipe I’ve been putting off trying because it seems like too much work to feed just one person. Invest in some good Tupperware for leftovers, light the candle, live your damn life!

Who knew a game-show lifeline could also function as a mental-health life preserver? When I first moved into my place alone, I worried that my lifelong tendency to self-isolate when things are hard would flare up without someone to physically share space with, but I’ve actually gotten better about reaching out when I need support, maybe because it’s just me and my dog (on the nights he’s not spending with his dad, that is). I still have some avoidant tendencies, but calling my besties to vent when solo living and my currently single status make me feel lonely has helped me realize that real emotional connection isn’t just about someone being there: It’s about letting someone be there for you, and doing your best to be there for them in return.

As it turns out, I’m kind of guarded about bringing dates over to my place; partly because a reactive, bark-y Maltipoo who hates strangers lives there half the time, but also because I’ve become unexpectedly protective of my domain. When I lived with a rotating cast of roommates in my twenties, it felt like no big deal to entertain a near-stranger in a bedroom that invariably consisted of a bare mattress, a stack of books and an empty iced-latte cup, but now that I’ve put time and energy into creating a home I love living alone, I have to really want someone to visit if I invite them over. (Don’t worry, I’m still making regrettable romantic choices every so often, I just go to their places instead of mine.)

I always assumed I’d get bored living alone without other people’s gossip and drama to entertain me. Sometimes I do, and you know what? It’s kind of great. Quitting weed has taught me that I don’t need to fill every dull moment with stimulation or numb out to avoid hard feelings, and living alone while weed-abstinent is a consistent exercise in filling time (although less of one than I feared it would be, given the whole “no canceling social plans” thing). Boredom has led me to start drawing again for the first time since I was a kid, perfect my French onion soup recipe, and even start doing stand-up at mercifully low-attendance open mics, so where else will it lead me, I wonder?

I am a devoted estate-sale and flea-market freak who’s lowkey addicted to trinkets, and while I’m trying to curb my spending (I need to pay my handybutch, after all), I’ve noticed that the cheapest items I own—from a vintage copy of Mary Ellman’s Thinking About Women anthology that a kind bookseller at Womb House Books gifted me to a $5 milk frother I scored during a MoMA Design Store sale to a $10 sculptural yellow dish I scored at the Long Beach Flea Market—are the ones that I tend to look at and sigh in contentment, thrilled to live in my very own space without having to accommodate anyone else’s items or design ideas. Minimalism is overrated!

I’ve always loved Ruth Reichl’s description of making herself a bare-bones omelet in a borrowed apartment in Paris and “thinking that I was being a guest to myself” in her 2001 memoir Comfort Me with Apples, and I try to embody that spirit every time I run a bath or choose a movie or make a meal in my studio, whether it’s a multi-step chili or a simple bowl of yogurt with fruit and Tamar Adler’s granola. I may not be able to host a crowd in my studio the way I could in previous living spaces, but that’s okay; as it turns out, I’m enough.

#6649. What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives

The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use.

Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique.

Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work.

Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone.

Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel.

Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing.

The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife.

We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review.

Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry.

Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku.

Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion.

The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point.

The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well.

We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife.

Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup.

We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl.

Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip.

Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar.

The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip.

When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion.

Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t.

We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

#6648. Best-Ever Pavlova

Pavlova is essentially a massive meringue that melts in your mouth. We top our version with whipped cream and fresh berries for an airy and fruity bite that will keep you coming back bite after bite. It may look like a complicated dessert made by only the best chefs, but it's surprisingly easy to make! You just need some patience. The key to perfection is drying it out, which requires you to leave it in a (turned-off) oven overnight after it bakes.

If you’re looking for something a bit more festive, check out our Christmas wreath pavlova for a holiday spin on the classic.

Arrange a rack in the center of the oven; preheat to 300°. In a large bowl, beat egg whites with a large pinch of salt on medium-high speed with a handheld mixer (or in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment) until foamy, which should take about one minute.

While beating, slowly add sugar and beat until meringue is thick and glossy, which should take about 7 minutes. Beat in vinegar, cornstarch, and vanilla until well combined.

Pile the meringue in the center of a parchment-lined baking sheet. Using a spatula or spoon, spread the mixture into an 8" circle. Make a small well in the center.

Transfer to the oven, and immediately reduce the oven temperature to 250°. Bake the meringue until set but still white, which should take about an hour. Turn off the oven and let the pavlova cool completely in the oven for at least 2 hours and up to overnight. Transfer cooled pavlova to a platter.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store the unassembled pavlova in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days, keeping it away from humidity. Once topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit, refrigerate and enjoy within a day, as the meringue will soften over time.
